analysis.title: A week with APEC consequences?
key_insights: A third US aircraft carrier has arrived in the Middle East and Israeli representatives met US officials to discuss new strikes. Trump reportedly told advisers he may not attack Iran absent new provocations, partly at the request of Saudi Arabia and Türkiye.

Houthis claim to have targeted an airport and financial centre in Riyadh, and Iran launched a drone strike at a US base in Bahrain, which Iran calls a response to hostile US actions. Ghalibaf says Iran still wants to discuss a peace deal if the US accepts Iran's 'logical conditions'.

Iranian officials say Tehran will not stay in a state of 'neither war nor peace' and that it may 'not wait for the US to attack first'. Deputy Minister Gharibabadi suggests the White House is using diplomacy to buy time for another attack.
The Houthis have forced the retreat of Yemen's forces and again control the Bab al-Mandeb strait. They say they are no threat to international shipping and will target only Saudi Arabian vessels.
Oil has risen off recent lows on Middle East tensions and reports that up to five ships hit mines in the Strait of Hormuz. The UK Maritime Trade Operations Centre has confirmed one attack.

Trump, Xi and Putin are to hold a trilateral meeting on the sidelines of the APEC summit in Shenzhen. No agenda has reportedly been agreed, China has avoided an active role in Russia-Ukraine talks, and Rabobank expects no immediate results.
US-China tensions remain high on trade and protectionism. A separate Trump-Xi meeting later in the week will likely be dominated by defence and protectionism.

The US-China trade truce expires in January. The US accuses China of not meeting its side of the deal, rare earths are not reaching the US at the desired pace, and a House China Select Committee report says China has undercut and monopolized various industries.

The US and China are trying to finalise a military accident-prevention agreement before the summit, but progress is slow because of differing views inside the US administration. A US agreement with Japan, Australia and the Philippines on a regional defence coordination centre raises the need for such an accord and complicates talks.

The affair between Nvidia's former CEO Huang and an alleged Chinese spy is accelerating US efforts to tighten AI chip export controls, with bipartisan congressional support for bills limiting overseas sales of advanced chips. Treasury Secretary Bessent calls for a 'dramatic shake-up' at Nvidia.

US allies have agreed to create a joint list of key technologies and AI supply lines needing protection from China, and the US reportedly plans to nominate tens of companies as 'national champions' for US AI adoption. Rabobank says these moves are bound to anger Beijing and could matter for equities as the AI trade regains footing.
The Anthropic IPO may prove the next test for AI appetite.

Week ahead: Monday brings Eurozone industrial production, the US Empire manufacturing index and Canadian inflation, with Fed Chair Warsh on a panel and fireside chat. Tuesday's main event is US October retail sales, alongside the German ZEW survey and UK wages.

Wednesday brings UK and Eurozone October inflation, with Eurozone HICP not expected to deviate much from the 4.0% preliminary estimate, plus US housing starts and the October FOMC minutes. Thursday covers labour markets (Eurozone labour costs, US jobless claims, Philly Fed and Kansas City Fed surveys). Friday features Japanese CPI, and Eurozone negotiated wages are the likely market focus.
